newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Japan presses Jakarta on controversial car policy.
newsitem.headline: Japan presses Jakarta on controversial car policy.

text.p: Japan pressed Indonesia on Friday over its controversial national car policy, repeating its threat to take the issue to the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

Visiting Trade and Industry Minister Shunpei Tsukahara told reporters after meeting President Suharto that the two countries were holding talks on the issue but Japan reserved the right to approach the world body for a resolution.

Indonesia announced in February that a company controlled by Suharto's youngest son would receive tax breaks to manufacture sedans in collaboration with South Korea's Kia Motors under a national car programme. It is the only manufacturer to be granted the privilege.
The company, PT Timor Putra Nasional, is required to raise local content to 60 percent within three years of starting operations but has been permitted to import an initial batch of cars duty-free.
The first consignment of cars landed at Jakarta's Tanjung Priok port last month and Japan had said it would complain to the WTO once the import was completed.

"We have not been able to reconfirm the duty-free customs clearance of the car in your country yet. Therefore, in the event such duty-free custom clearance is confirmed, we may consider the possibility of requesting a full consultation based on WTO agreements. We will keep that in prespective," Tsukahara said.

Japan and the United States have previously said the policy violates WTO regulations and discriminates against existing joint-venture car manufacturers in Indonesia, most of which have Japanese or U.S. partners.
The tax breaks enable the Timor Putra car to be sold at about half the sticker price of comparable sedans now available in Indonesia.

"The exemption of import duty on such finished cars, and the exemption of luxury tax on such imports, could possibly mean violation of article one of GATT (the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade)," said Tsukahara, who is in Jakarta for consultations with counterparts from the Association of South East Asian nations (ASEAN).
"So far, we have continued talks between the two countries under bilateral auspices. Therefore we will continue to consider this as one possible alternative available to us."
Indonesian Trade and Industry Minister Tungky Ariwibowo said Jakarta was prepared to appear before the WTO.
"I think we can manage to overcome this, we are prepared for any possibility," Ariwibowo told reporters.
He said more companies could be given similar tax breaks under the scheme, but only after three years.
"The president mentioned that it is not possible for one company to satisfy the whole market of Indonesia, this is impossible. There is plenty of room for other companies," Ariwibowo said.
"We have already said that this company will get the benefit for three years. After three years there is a possibility for a second company to join the programme," Ariwibowo said.
